newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Political rifts add to Albania lawlessness.
newsitem.headline: Political rifts add to Albania lawlessness.

text.p: Rifts opened in President Sali Berisha's right-wing party on Friday, aggravating the crisis in lawless Albania as it prepares for the arrival of an Italian-led force to protect aid.

A faction of about 20 Democratic parliamentarians signed a statement saying they would no longer "accept the dictat of the president". This was the strongest criticism yet of Berisha from within his own ranks since Albania slid towards anarchy last month.
The group stopped short of a formal break, saying a solution to Albania's woes "exists within the programme of the Democratic Party". A new general election is due to be held in June.
Berisha's party won 122 seats in the 140-seat parliament in elections last year and would retain a stranglehold on the legislature even without the new faction's support.
Political in-fighting adds to the problems faced by a 6,000-strong Italian-led force that the Italian foreign ministry said on Friday it expected to start deploying in the week starting April 14.

Southern Albania is in rebel hands after last month's uprising, with looting and banditry rife. Rebel councils are demanding the resignation of Berisha, blamed for the collapse of savings schemes at the root of Albania's unrest.

"The greatest part of the blame for the crisis lies with him (Berisha)," said former deputy prime minister Dashamir Shehi, a leader of the breakaway Democratic group who accused Berisha of trying to amass too much power.

"This is a huge crisis, the worst we have faced, because it is economic, political, moral, a crisis of faith in the institutions," he told Italian television. He said the document could offer an alternative to Berisha and the opposition Socialist party.
In the rebel-held southern port of Vlore, Defence Minister Shaqir Vukaj suggested on Friday that French or Spanish soldiers in a 6,000-strong Italian-led force could protect aid.

Vukaj visited the port in a bid to calm recent anger with Rome over the sinking of a refugee ship after a collision with an Italian corvette in which Albania says at least 80 people drowned. Many of the 34 survivors accused the navy of ramming.

"I would suggest that French or Spanish soldiers come to Vlore," he said after talks with local authorities including the rebel-led "salvation committee" heading the town since central control collapsed in Albania last month.

"The government and the Italian government will assist Vlore," he said. The port is one of two that the U.N.-approved force is meant to secure as bridgeheads to ensure that deliveries of food and medicines get through.
He also said that it "would not be good for Greek soldiers to come to the south", close to the border with Greece.

In Tirana, a group of three representatives of Vlore council visited the Italian ambassador to reassure Italy that the town would welcome them despite angry denunciations by many citizens earlier in the week.

The sinking badly complicated Italy's plans to lead the U.N.-approved force of at least eight nations -- Italy, France, Greece, Turkey, Spain, Romania, Austria and Denmark -- to protect food and medical supplies to the Balkan state.

In Tirana, the military academy reopened with a ceremony attended by chief of staff Adem Copani, who inspected about 200 cadets on a dusty parade ground. It was the first school of any type to reopen after the violence.

In Fushe-Kruje, north of the capital, a man was detained on suspicion of massacring six members of his family. The man was suspected of shooting dead his parents, two sisters and his brother and sister-in-law after a drunken rampage.
